rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The moderate temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to measure how the two critical pairs respond to a shallower slope. The last peak should remain near or below 10 minutes, allowing improved resolution without a substantial time penalty.

The critical pair improved substantially with a shallower gradient. Raising the starting organic fraction narrows the gradient window and further reduces its slope while aiming to keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Lengthen the current gradient by one grid step to improve the remaining critical pair. The 1.38-minute margin below the time-penalty threshold should accommodate this change while potentially reaching full resolution.
Injection 4 already achieves the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Raise temperature one step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation and measure the critical pair’s temperature sensitivity.

The critical pair is strongly temperature-sensitive and may separate again after an elution-order reversal. Test 55 C at the same gradient to assess that possibility and seek a faster separation, retaining injection 4 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Make the 55 C gradient one step shallower to improve the newly critical pair at R 1.41. This should keep the last peak below 10 minutes, while testing whether the other close pair retains adequate resolution.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction improves separation of the early critical pair enough to permit a shorter gradient at 55 C. Injection 7 remains a fully resolved benchmark while this explores a faster elution window.

Shorten injection 8 by one gradient-duration step to test the speed limit of this fully resolved window. This isolates the slope response of both close pairs while aiming to reduce the last-peak time below 8 minutes.

Lower the endpoint to make the 12-minute gradient shallower and recover resolution of the R 1.29 pair. The last peak should still elute within the gradient, potentially giving full resolution slightly faster than injection 8.

Test a lower starting organic fraction with a faster gradient, since lowering phi0 previously helped the early critical pair. This explores whether full resolution can be retained with a last-peak time near 7 minutes.

Test the upper temperature limit with a shorter gradient to explore separation after a possible reversal of the early critical pair. This is a speed-focused exploratory run; injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Explore low-temperature selectivity with a fast gradient, since the high-temperature branch has encountered a different limiting pair. This tests whether temperature-driven order changes can provide a shorter fully resolved separation than the current 8.00-minute benchmark.

Explore a faster, higher-starting-organic window at 55 C to test whether the limiting pair separates after an order reversal. The first two peaks will also be checked for excessive compression near the dead time.

Refine the fastest fully resolved window with a slope between injections 9 and 10, targeting just enough resolution for the limiting pair. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, and the last peak should arrive around 7.8 minutes.

Explore the fast-gradient side of the order reversal at 60 C, using a lower starting fraction than injection 14 to protect the first pair. This tests a substantially faster alternative while retaining injection 15 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Lengthen injection 11 by one step to recover the early critical pair’s resolution while checking that the other close pair remains above 1.5. This lower-starting window may achieve full resolution slightly faster than injection 15.

Test intermediate-temperature selectivity with a fast gradient to seek a balance between the two competing critical pairs. Injection 17 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, with the maximum CRF already secured.

Test a modestly cooler temperature with a shorter gradient than the successful 40 C method, seeking improved selectivity for its limiting pair. This explores a remaining temperature region while preserving injection 17 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test whether a higher starting fraction at 50 C improves the later critical pair while a shallower gradient resolves the earlier one. The cooler temperature should also help retain the first two peaks compared with injection 14, potentially yielding a faster fully resolved method.

Test a gradient slope just steeper than injection 15 to locate the full-resolution speed limit in this window. The early critical pair is expected to be near R 1.5, with a last-peak time around 7.6 minutes.

Trim injection 17’s endpoint while preserving its successful gradient slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute. All peaks previously eluted before this shorter gradient would end, so this should retain maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient and lower final organic content.

Increase the slope slightly from the fastest fully resolved method to test whether its R 1.59 pair can tolerate further acceleration. This brackets the speed limit of the low-starting-organic window; injection 22 remains a confirmed maximum-score fallback.

Back off from injection 23 to the proven slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute, using a new endpoint-duration combination. This should recover full resolution and retain the 7.60-minute last-peak time of the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Preserve injection 10’s fully resolving slope while trimming the endpoint to just above its estimated last-peak elution fraction. This should retain CRF 1.000 with an 8-minute programmed gradient and a slightly larger minimum-resolution margin than injection 22.
